introduction: This foundational level explores the genesis of Rent Control legislation in India. Originally enacted to combat extreme housing shortages and exorbitant rent hikes after World War II and the Partition, these state-specific laws operate as exceptions to the general Transfer of Property Act (TPA).

core_concepts.title: The Philosophy of Rent Control
core_concepts.description:
Rent Control Acts are pieces of 'beneficial legislation' designed primarily to protect tenants. They serve two main purposes:
1. Protection against Arbitrary Eviction: Landlords cannot evict tenants merely because the lease agreement has expired. They MUST prove specific statutory grounds.
2. Fixation of Standard Rent: Landlords cannot charge whatever the market dictates; they can only charge a statutorily fixed 'Standard Rent', preventing rack-renting.

core_concepts.title: The 'Statutory Tenant'
core_concepts.description:
A deeply tested concept in Judiciary exams. Under the general Transfer of Property Act, once a lease expires, the tenant must leave. 
- The Rent Control Rule: Even after the contractual lease expires, if the tenant continues to possess the premises and pays rent, they become a **'Statutory Tenant'**. The law steps in to protect their tenancy, and they can only be evicted on the specific grounds listed in the Rent Act.

core_concepts.title: Standard Rent / Fair Rent
core_concepts.description:
The maximum rent a landlord is legally allowed to charge. 
- Mechanism: It is calculated by a Rent Controller based on a specific statutory formula (usually a percentage of the actual cost of construction and the market price of the land at the time construction commenced). Any agreement to pay rent higher than the Standard Rent is legally void.

core_concepts.title: Exemptions from Rent Control
core_concepts.description:
Not all properties fall under Rent Control. To encourage new construction and commercial investments, states exempt certain premises. 
- Common Exemptions (e.g., Delhi Rent Control Act): (1) Premises whose monthly rent exceeds ₹3,500. (2) Newly constructed buildings (exempt for the first 10 years). (3) Premises owned by the Government.

important_entities.name: The Rent Controller
important_entities.significance: Under Rent Control Acts, regular civil courts usually do not hear eviction suits. A specialized authority, the 'Rent Controller', is appointed to adjudicate disputes between landlords and tenants expeditiously, focusing on rent fixation and eviction petitions.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a statutory tenant dies, does the landlord automatically get the property back? **NO**. Under most state Acts (like the DRC Act), statutory tenancy is heritable. The legal heirs (spouse, son, daughter) who were normally living with the tenant at the time of death inherit the right to continue living there as statutory tenants.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: No Rack Renting + No Arbitrary Eviction
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The entire legal structure of any state Rent Act rests on these two protective pillars.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary Prelims question asks 'Which Act governs a tenancy if the monthly rent is ₹5,000 in Delhi?', select **The Transfer of Property Act, 1882**. Because it exceeds ₹3,500, the Delhi Rent Control Act ceases to apply.
